Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I try to push them out of my mind
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

vignette:
At 36, Linh Tran came to treatment after months of telling herself that if she just stayed busy enough, the worst moments would pass on their own. She was a Vietnamese American urban planner, living with her partner and working in a city office where her days were usually structured around zoning maps, transit corridors, and community meetings. Before seeking help, she had spent years trying to keep her experience as a relief worker in a war zone partitioned off from the rest of her life, as if it were something that had happened to another woman with her face and voice but not really to her.

The event she returned to, when she could bear to, took place while she was assigned to a relief operation in a rural area scarred by fighting. The camp and supply routes ran along open, green stretches of land that should have looked peaceful from a distance. Instead, Linh remembered that natural landscape as the setting for terror: uneven ground, brush and tree cover, the sense that danger could be hidden in any direction. On the day that stayed with her most forcefully, shouting broke out without warning. Voices rose fast—urgent, panicked, overlapping in a language she only partly understood—and people began moving abruptly around her. She remembered the shock of bodies turning, running, crouching, grabbing for cover, and her own instant sense that something catastrophic was happening. What remained most vivid was not a tidy sequence but fragments: the volume of the shouting, sudden motion at the edge of her vision, the raw feeling of being trapped in exposed terrain. When she tried to tell the story now, she would begin with one detail and then lose the thread, stopping mid-sentence, looking confused and frustrated, as if the scene had broken apart in her hands.

In the weeks after she returned to the United States, Linh found that ordinary things could pull that place around her again. Old photos were especially dangerous. It did not even have to be a picture from deployment; sometimes an image from that period, or simply seeing herself from those years, was enough to make her feel abruptly transported. She described moments of suddenly acting as if she were back there, her body tightening and orienting toward escape before she had fully registered where she actually was. Being in nature could do the same. A weekend hike with her partner, meant to be relaxing, became unbearable when the trail opened into scrubby, sunlit terrain that resembled the landscape where she had worked. She went silent, scanned the surroundings, and then insisted they turn back without being able to explain why. Shouting was the most immediate trigger. If raised voices broke out on the street below her apartment or at a tense public meeting at work, she felt her heart slam and her body react as if she were under threat in that open rural setting again.

Linh had come to believe that the only way to get through the day was to never let her mind go still. She filled every quiet interval with podcasts, work emails, background television, extra tasks—anything to keep from drifting toward memory. When images or sensations forced their way in, she tried to push them out immediately. If that failed and the feelings became overwhelming, she sometimes hurt herself physically, describing it as a way to release pressure she could not otherwise contain. She did not present this dramatically; she spoke of it with shame and practicality, as something she turned to when she felt cornered by her own mind.

Her memory of the war zone also felt estranged from her. She would say it was like looking at someone else’s experience, close enough to unsettle her but not fully hers. Yet when recall broke through that distance, what surged up was intense rage. She was not always able to put words to what or whom the rage was aimed at; it arrived hot and immediate, leaving her jaw clenched and her whole body activated. At work, this meant she was constantly managing herself. In planning meetings, if someone stood up too quickly beside her chair or gestured suddenly across a conference table, she reacted sharply, shoulders jerking and breath catching, then sat embarrassed and defensive. She began choosing seats against the wall and avoiding some in-person meetings when she could. Nights were no easier. She had trouble falling asleep because she felt she needed to stay alert, as though letting go into sleep would be a mistake. Her partner noticed that she listened for sounds in the apartment and hallway long after they had gone to bed.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but the narrowing of her life. She and her partner had stopped going on the outdoor trips they once enjoyed. She was becoming harder to reach at home and more brittle at work, exhausted from vigilance and from the effort of keeping her mind occupied every waking hour. In sessions, she said she was frightened by how quickly the past could overtake the present and by how little command she seemed to have when it did. At the same time, she said she wanted, more than anything, to be able to remember what happened without either disappearing from it entirely or being thrown back into it as if it were happening again.
